## Data

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(fpp2)
library(forecast)
df <- read.csv("Unemployment in America Per US State.csv", check.names = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
names(df) <- c("fips","state","year","month","pop","lf","lf_pct","emp","emp_pct","unemp","urate")
nj <- subset(df, state == "New Jersey")
nj$urate <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(nj$urate))
njts <- ts(nj$urate, start = c(1976, 1), frequency = 12)
njts[is.na(njts)] <- (5.2 + 5.4) / 2   # Oct 2025 missing (shutdown): average of Sep and Nov
plot(njts, main = "New Jersey unemployment rate", ylab = "%")
ndiffs(njts)
tsdisplay(njts)

njtsdiff1 <- diff(njts, differences = 1)
plot(njtsdiff1)
tsdisplay(njtsdiff1)
```


The time series is the monthly New Jersey unemployment rate from January 1976 to November 2025 (seasonally adjusted). ndiffs() = 1, so the series needs one difference to be stationary. The ACF decays slowly, which shows a trend. COVID pushed the rate to 15.4% in April 2020.

## Perform ARIMA

```{r}
njts_model <- njts
window(njts_model, start = c(2020, 3), end = c(2021, 12)) <- NA   # remove the COVID shock
auto_fit <- auto.arima(njts_model, trace = TRUE, stepwise = FALSE)
auto_fit
```

## 1. Explain the output

auto.arima tested many models (the trace list) and chose ARIMA(1,1,2)(2,0,0)[12] because it had the lowest AICc. The non-seasonal part (1,1,2) means 1 autoregressive term, 1 difference and 2 moving-average terms. The seasonal part (2,0,0)[12] adds 2 seasonal AR terms at lags 12 and 24. The ar1 coefficient
